parts.text: While Merlin and Morgan were away,
parts.meaning: When Merlin and Morgan were not there,

parts.text: Teddy accidentally put a spell on Penny,
parts.meaning: Teddy put a spell on Penny by mistake,

parts.text: Merlin’s beloved penguin,
parts.meaning: the penguin that Merlin loves,

parts.text: and turned her into a stone statue.
parts.meaning: and made her become a stone statue.

sentences.grammar: "While" + past tense tells what was happening at that time. "Merlin's beloved penguin" is put between commas to say more about Penny.

sentences.context: They have just returned from a magic tree house journey to India, where they found the first thing: an emerald in the shape of a rose.
sentences.simple: They just came back from a trip to India in the magic tree house. There they found the first thing, an emerald that looks like a rose.
sentences.main: They have just returned from a journey to India.

parts.text: They have just returned from a magic tree house journey to India,
parts.meaning: They came back a very short time ago from a trip to India,

parts.text: where they found the first thing:
parts.job: What happened in India ("where" = in India).
parts.meaning: and in India they found the first thing:

parts.text: an emerald in the shape of a rose.
parts.job: What the first thing is (after the colon).
parts.meaning: a green jewel that looks like a rose.

sentences.grammar: "Have just + past participle" = a very short time ago. "Where" joins a new part about the place. A colon (:) comes before the answer or the list.

sentences.context: The houses they passed were all quiet, but the world of nature was awake with birdsong and dogs barking in the distance.
sentences.simple: All the houses were quiet, but nature was awake: birds were singing and dogs were barking far away.
sentences.main: The houses were all quiet, but the world of nature was awake.

parts.text: The houses they passed were all quiet,
parts.job: First idea ("they passed" tells which houses).
parts.meaning: The houses they walked by were all quiet,

parts.text: but the world of nature was awake
parts.meaning: but nature was already awake

parts.text: with birdsong and dogs barking in the distance.
parts.meaning: with birds singing and dogs barking far away.

sentences.grammar: "The houses they passed" = the houses that they passed ("that" can be left out). "But" joins two opposite ideas.

sentences.context: It was hard to see in the shadowy dark, but they were so familiar with the path to the tallest oak that they quickly found their way.
sentences.simple: It was dark and hard to see, but they knew the path to the tall oak tree so well that they found it fast.
sentences.main: They were so familiar with the path that they quickly found their way.

parts.text: It was hard to see in the shadowy dark,
parts.meaning: It was dark, so it was hard to see,

parts.text: but they were so familiar with the path to the tallest oak
parts.meaning: but they knew the path to the tallest oak very well

parts.text: that they quickly found their way.
parts.meaning: and so they found the way fast.

sentences.grammar: "So + adjective + that ..." tells a result: "so familiar that they quickly found their way." "It was hard to see" uses "it" as an empty subject.

sentences.context: For hundreds of years, the monks at this Swiss monastery have welcomed cold and weary travelers who are crossing the pass.
sentences.simple: For hundreds of years, the monks in this monastery in Switzerland have helped cold, tired travelers who go over the mountain pass.
sentences.main: The monks have welcomed cold and weary travelers.

parts.text: For hundreds of years,
parts.meaning: For many hundreds of years,

parts.text: the monks at this Swiss monastery have welcomed cold and weary travelers
parts.meaning: the monks here have welcomed cold, tired travelers

parts.text: who are crossing the pass.
parts.meaning: that are going over the pass.

sentences.grammar: "Have welcomed" + "for hundreds of years" = it started long ago and is still true now. "Who are crossing" tells which travelers.

sentences.context: Directly above them on the mountain, big blocks of snow were breaking into smaller chunks and sliding down the slope.
sentences.simple: Right above them on the mountain, big pieces of snow were breaking into smaller pieces and moving down fast.
sentences.main: Big blocks of snow were breaking into smaller chunks and sliding down the slope.

parts.text: Directly above them on the mountain,
parts.meaning: Right over their heads on the mountain,

parts.text: big blocks of snow were breaking into smaller chunks
parts.meaning: big pieces of snow were breaking into smaller pieces

parts.text: and sliding down the slope.
parts.job: What else the snow was doing.
parts.meaning: and moving down the side of the mountain.

sentences.grammar: Past continuous ("were breaking ... and sliding") shows two actions going on at the same time. "Directly above them" = right above them.

sentences.context: He tried to stand, but a giant wave of soft, powdery snow blew over him, burying him completely.
sentences.simple: He tried to get up, but a huge wave of soft snow came over him and covered him all over.
sentences.main: A giant wave of snow blew over him.

parts.text: He tried to stand,
parts.meaning: He tried to get up,

parts.text: but a giant wave of soft, powdery snow blew over him,
parts.meaning: but a huge wave of soft snow came over him,

parts.text: burying him completely.
parts.meaning: and it covered him all over.

sentences.grammar: An "-ing" part after a comma ("burying him completely") tells the result of the action before it.

sentences.context: Jack and Annie could walk without help, but they both limped a little as they followed Brother Michael down the hall into the dimly lit parlor.
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie could walk alone, but they both walked a little badly as they went after Brother Michael to the dark sitting room.
sentences.main: They both limped a little as they followed Brother Michael.

parts.text: Jack and Annie could walk without help,
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie could walk by themselves,

parts.text: but they both limped a little
parts.meaning: but they both walked a little unevenly because they were hurt

parts.text: as they followed Brother Michael down the hall into the dimly lit parlor.
parts.meaning: while they went with Brother Michael down the hall into the sitting room with little light.

sentences.grammar: "As" can mean "while; at the same time". "Dimly lit" = with only a little light.

sentences.context: Once they hear the voice of the snow, as we call it, their noses lead them in the right direction.
sentences.simple: When the dogs hear what the monks call "the voice of the snow," their noses show them where to go.
sentences.main: Their noses lead them in the right direction.

parts.text: Once they hear the voice of the snow,
parts.meaning: As soon as the dogs hear the voice of the snow,

parts.text: as we call it,
parts.meaning: which is what we call it,

parts.text: their noses lead them in the right direction.
parts.meaning: their noses take them the right way.

sentences.grammar: "Once" can mean "as soon as; after". "As we call it" = that is the name we give it.

sentences.context: Barry jumped back onto Jack’s bed and started pawing at the blanket, trying to dig Jack out from underneath.
sentences.simple: Barry jumped onto Jack's bed again and began to scratch at the blanket with his paws, as if he wanted to dig Jack out.
sentences.main: Barry jumped back onto Jack’s bed and started pawing at the blanket.

parts.text: Barry jumped back onto Jack’s bed
parts.meaning: Barry jumped onto Jack's bed again

parts.text: and started pawing at the blanket,
parts.meaning: and began to scratch the blanket with his paws,

parts.text: trying to dig Jack out from underneath.
parts.meaning: because he wanted to dig Jack out from under it.

sentences.grammar: "Start + -ing" = begin to do. "Trying to ..." after a comma tells what Barry wanted to do.

sentences.context: “Because he has a very independent spirit, and none of us has the time to give him the extra training he needs,” said Brother Michael.
sentences.simple: "Because he likes to do what he wants, and none of us has time to give him the extra training he needs," said Brother Michael.
sentences.main: He has a very independent spirit, and none of us has the time.

parts.text: “Because he has a very independent spirit,
parts.meaning: "Because he likes to do things his own way,

parts.text: and none of us has the time
parts.meaning: and nobody here has the time

parts.text: to give him the extra training he needs,”
parts.meaning: to teach him all the extra things he needs to learn,"

parts.text: said Brother Michael.
parts.meaning: said Brother Michael.

sentences.grammar: "None of us" takes a singular verb here: "none of us has". "The training he needs" = the training that he needs.

sentences.context: He was warm, his body was sturdy and strong, and he could smell and hear a whole new world of scents and sounds.
sentences.simple: He felt warm, his body felt strong, and he could smell and hear many new smells and sounds.
sentences.main: He was warm and strong, and he could smell and hear a whole new world.

parts.text: He was warm,
parts.meaning: He felt warm,

parts.text: his body was sturdy and strong,
parts.meaning: his body was strong and solid,

parts.text: and he could smell and hear a whole new world of scents and sounds.
parts.meaning: and he could smell and hear many new smells and sounds.

sentences.grammar: A list of three ideas: "A, B, and C." Each part has its own subject and verb.

sentences.context: With barely a pause, Barry barreled on, his paws and powerful chest plowing through the snow, clearing a passage.
sentences.simple: Barry hardly stopped. He ran on fast, and his paws and strong chest pushed through the snow and made a way.

parts.text: With barely a pause,
parts.meaning: Almost without stopping,

parts.text: Barry barreled on,
parts.meaning: Barry kept running fast and hard,

parts.text: his paws and powerful chest plowing through the snow,
parts.meaning: with his paws and strong chest pushing through the snow,

parts.text: clearing a passage.
parts.meaning: making a way through it.

sentences.grammar: After the main idea, a noun + "-ing" part ("his paws ... plowing") tells more about the action. "Barely" = almost not.

sentences.context: His eyes searched the pass for signs of the tree house, until finally he thought he saw it: brown wood nestled on a slope among gray boulders.
sentences.simple: He looked all over the pass for the tree house, and at last he thought he saw it: brown wood sitting safely on a slope between big gray rocks.
sentences.main: His eyes searched the pass for signs of the tree house.

parts.text: His eyes searched the pass for signs of the tree house,
parts.meaning: He looked all over the pass for the tree house,

parts.text: until finally he thought he saw it:
parts.meaning: and at last he thought he saw it:

parts.text: brown wood nestled on a slope among gray boulders.
parts.meaning: brown wood sitting safely on a slope between big gray rocks.

sentences.grammar: "Search a place for something" = look all over a place to find it. "Until" tells when the searching stopped.

all set.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

all the way.example: I should have closed the door all the way!”
all the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

along with.example: He put them into his backpack along with the emerald rose.
along with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that...
as if.example: He felt as if he were drowning—until he finally pushed his head up through the snow into the cold air.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as soon as.meaning: At the moment that; right after.

as soon as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

as well as.example: “We have a dog kennel and a chapel, as well as a library filled with books and exhibits of rocks, minerals, and butterflies.
as well as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at all.meaning: In any way. "Not ... at all" means "not even a little".
at all.example: While they were gone, no time at all passed back in Frog Creek.
at all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at least.meaning: Used to say one thing is good, even when other things are bad.
at least.example: “Well, at least they sent the tree house,” said Jack.
at least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at the same time.example: He wanted to lie down, but at the same time he was hungry and cold.
at the same time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

back off.example: A man shouted, and the dogs backed off.
back off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: Jack felt as if he were about to be licked to death!
be about to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

be on your way.meaning: To leave and go. "I must be on my way" means I must go now.
be on your way.example: “Thank you, but I fear I must be on my way,” Napoléon Bonaparte said.
be on your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be supposed to.meaning: Should; to be expected to do something ("the exact place we're supposed to go").
be supposed to.example: “That must be the exact place we’re supposed to go,” said Jack.
be supposed to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

belong to.meaning: If a thing belongs to you, it is yours.
belong to.example: Jack and Annie eventually found out that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay, a magical librarian from the legendary realm of Camelot.
belong to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

bits and pieces.example: All around the room were bits and pieces of paper.
bits and pieces.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

blow out.meaning: To stop a flame by blowing on it.
blow out.example: Then he blew out the lantern flame and pulled up his wool blanket.
blow out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break loose.meaning: To get free from someone or something that is holding you.
break loose.example: But the dog broke loose from the monk and ran around the room.
break loose.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break someone's heart.meaning: To make someone very, very sad.
break someone's heart.example: It will break his heart to leave.”
break someone's heart.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break the spell.meaning: To end a magic spell, so things become normal again.
break the spell.example: “We have to find the second thing to break the spell that turned Penny to stone!”
break the spell.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bring out.meaning: To help something hidden inside someone to show itself ("bring out Barry's instincts").
bring out.example: You helped bring out Barry’s instincts to be a rescue dog, Jack.
bring out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

burst into.meaning: To come into a room suddenly and fast.
burst into.example: Just as he grabbed it, the door banged open, and a Saint Bernard dog burst into the room.
burst into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

burst out laughing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

by the time.meaning: "By the time they reached the tree" means at the moment when they reached it (and not before).
by the time.example: By the time they had emptied their bowls, Jack was feeling much better.
by the time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up to.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up to.example: Annie caught up to Jack and peered into the room.
catch up to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up with.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up with.example: Then the rosy-faced monk hurried off to catch up with the others.
catch up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

change into.meaning: To become something different, often by magic ("We can change into anything we want").
change into.example: We can change into anything we want for an hour.”
change into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

change out of.meaning: To take off some clothes and put on other clothes.
change out of.example: Annie left the room, and Jack quickly changed out of his pajamas and into jeans and a sweatshirt.
change out of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come back.example: “We have to go to the tree house and come back before it’s time to get ready for school.”
come back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come on.meaning: "Come on!" means "Hurry!", "Let's go!" or "Please do it!"
come on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

dig out.meaning: To get someone or something out from under snow or earth by digging.
dig out.example: He could see that he’d been mostly dug out of the snow, but he still couldn’t feel or move his body.
dig out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

each other.meaning: Used to say that each one does something to the other one.
each other.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

even if.meaning: It does not matter if this happens; the result is the same.
even if.example: “And even if you had, we don’t have time now.
even if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

except for.example: The dining hall was empty now, except for Jack and Annie.
except for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

excuse me.meaning: A polite way to start talking to someone you do not know, or to say sorry.
excuse me.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

faster and faster.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you understand it or find the answer.
figure out.example: “But we have to look in our book,” said Jack, “and try to figure out—”
figure out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.example: Jack and Annie eventually found out that the tree house belonged to Morgan le Fay, a magical librarian from the legendary realm of Camelot.
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find your way.meaning: To find the right way to a place.
find your way.example: They can find their way to a person buried six feet down.”
find your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

first and foremost.meaning: Most of all; more than anything else.
first and foremost.example: “But I am a botanist first and foremost.”
first and foremost.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly.
flip through.example: Jack flipped through it until he came to a section with photos of plants and animals.
flip through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for the first time.meaning: As something new, never done or felt before.
for the first time.example: For the first time, Jack got a good look at the huge, panting dogs.
for the first time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for your information.meaning: "For your information" = I want you to know this (often said a little crossly).
for your information.example: “For your information, I just read a book on training dogs.
for your information.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fresh air.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

from side to side.meaning: Moving to the left and then to the right, again and again.
from side to side.example: He wiggled and rocked from side to side.
from side to side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get a good look.meaning: To see something well and clearly.
get a good look.example: For the first time, Jack got a good look at the huge, panting dogs.
get a good look.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get going.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get lost.meaning: To not know where you are or how to get back.
get lost.example: I am certain he would dash off to explore the mountains and get lost in the snow.”
get lost.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get ready.meaning: To make yourself ready for something.
get ready.example: “We have to go to the tree house and come back before it’s time to get ready for school.”
get ready.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get started.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get to work.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go after.meaning: To follow someone to catch them.
go after.example: She started to go after him.
go after.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go back.example: “Maybe we should go back and look through the monastery again,” said Jack.
go back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

good luck.meaning: I hope things go well for you.
good luck.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

good point.meaning: "Good point" means "That is a good idea" or "You are right about that."
good point.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

grow up.meaning: To become an adult; to be a child who is getting older.
grow up.example: “But he is a two-hundred-pound dog who needs to grow up.”
grow up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

had better.meaning: "We'd better go" means we should go, or something bad may happen.
had better.example: “We’d better go answer it,” said Annie.
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

half asleep.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have a feeling.meaning: To think something is true or will happen, without knowing for sure.
have a feeling.example: And I have a feeling that he—or someone else here—is going to help us.”
have a feeling.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

have no idea.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold on.meaning: 1. To hold something firmly ("held on tightly"). 2. "Hold on!" = Wait a moment!
hold on.example: This time he held on tight and pulled him into the kitchen.
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold up.meaning: To lift something and hold it high, so people can see it.
hold up.example: Father Laurent gently held up a cluster of tiny pink flowers.
hold up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, often because you are afraid or excited.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hurt someone's feelings.meaning: To make someone sad by saying or doing something unkind.
hurt someone's feelings.example: “I really hurt his feelings when I said bad, bad, bad.
hurt someone's feelings.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

i'm afraid.meaning: "I'm afraid ..." is a polite way to say something sad or bad: "I am sorry to say ..."
i'm afraid.example: “Um, I’m afraid your officer isn’t here,” said Annie.
i'm afraid.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

if only.meaning: "If only ..." means "I wish ..." (but it is not true).
if only.example: Live its meaning for yourself, if only for an hour.
if only.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in a daze.meaning: Not able to think clearly, as if half asleep.
in a daze.example: Jack and Annie sat on wooden chairs and stared in a daze at the crackling fire.
in a daze.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. People say "in fact" to add something more surprising.
in fact.example: In fact, we recently went to India and studied the Taj Mahal.
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in front of.example: As they carefully put one foot in front of the other, a strange sound came from above: whumph!
in front of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the dead of night.meaning: In the middle of the night, when it is very dark and quiet.
in the dead of night.example: No one should ever be caught on these mountains in the dead of night.”
in the dead of night.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the distance.meaning: Far away, but you can still see or hear it.
in the distance.example: The houses they passed were all quiet, but the world of nature was awake with birdsong and dogs barking in the distance.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the shape of.meaning: Having the form of something ("a hat in the shape of a triangle").
in the shape of.example: They have just returned from a magic tree house journey to India, where they found the first thing: an emerald in the shape of a rose.
in the shape of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

just as.meaning: 1. At the same moment that. 2. In the same way that.
just as.example: Just as he grabbed it, the door banged open, and a Saint Bernard dog burst into the room.
just as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep in step with.meaning: To walk at the same speed as someone, moving your feet at the same time.
keep in step with.example: He moved quickly, keeping in step with Barry’s prancing gait.
keep in step with.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

kind of.meaning: 1. A little; quite. (Friendly talk.) 2. "All kinds of" = many different types of ("all kinds of fish").
kind of.example: “I feel kind of bad for yelling.”
kind of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

known as.meaning: Called by a name. "She became known as the Angel" means people started to call her that.
known as.example: “This is Caltha palustris, better known as marsh marigold,” he said.
known as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

lead the way.meaning: To go first and show others where to go.
lead the way.example: The three dogs led the way over the snowy pass, snorting and sneezing and panting.
lead the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let go of.meaning: To stop holding someone or something.
let go of.example: When they let go of him, he started to fall.
let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

lie down.meaning: To put your body flat, for example on a bed. (Past tense: lay down.)
lie down.example: He wanted to lie down, but at the same time he was hungry and cold.
lie down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look around.meaning: To look at the things or places around you, often to find something.
look around.example: He sat up, put his glasses on, and looked around the white-walled room.
look around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look for.example: But where do we go to look for it?”
look for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look up ("Jack looked up"). 2. To look for a fact in a book ("I'd better look this up").
look up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make sense.meaning: To be easy to understand; to seem right.
make sense.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make sure.meaning: To check, or to do something, so that you are sure about something.
make sure.example: “No, I just want to make sure he’s okay,” said Annie.
make sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make your way.meaning: To go somewhere, often slowly or past many people.
make your way.example: “Consul Napoléon hoped he had made his way here on his own.”
make your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

most of all.example: And most of all, he felt a wild joy.
most of all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

night and day.example: He will cry night and day if he has to leave us.
night and day.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no kidding.meaning: "No kidding!" means "That is really true!" or "I really agree!" (Friendly talk.)

no kidding.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no problem.meaning: "No problem" = It is OK; I can do it easily.
no problem.example: Barry sneezed as if to say, No problem!
no problem.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no sign of.meaning: "There was no sign of ..." means you could not see it anywhere.
no sign of.example: There was no sign of him.
no sign of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

of course.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, brother.meaning: What you say when you feel a little tired of something or a little annoyed. It is not about a real brother.
oh, brother.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, man.meaning: What you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. It is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a man.
oh, man.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, my.meaning: "Oh, my!" = what you say when you are surprised, like "Oh!" or "Wow!"
oh, my.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, right.meaning: "Oh, right" = "Oh, I see; now I remember."
